questions.q: What is the core difference between slippage and market impact?
options: They are the same cost measured in different units
Slippage is driven by the market moving between decision and fill regardless of your size; market impact is a cost your own order size causes by moving the price while it fills
Market impact only applies to options trading
Slippage only matters for high-frequency strategies
questions.explain: Slippage can happen even with a tiny order, driven by general market movement. Market impact specifically results from an order being large enough, relative to available liquidity, to move the price against the trader while filling.

questions.q: In the square-root market impact model `impact ≈ sigma * sqrt(Q / ADV)`, what happens to impact cost if order size Q is increased 4x while ADV stays constant?
options: Impact cost increases 4x
Impact cost increases 16x
Impact cost increases 2x (the square root of 4)
Impact cost stays the same
questions.explain: Because impact scales with the square root of the participation rate (Q/ADV), a 4x increase in order size produces roughly a sqrt(4) = 2x increase in impact cost, not a proportional 4x increase.

questions.q: Why does a backtest run only at a small, 'illustrative' position size fail to reveal market impact costs?
options: Small orders are always free to execute
A small order doesn't consume enough liquidity to move the price, so the impact cost that would appear at larger size simply never shows up
Market impact only applies to small orders, not large ones
Backtests cannot model any transaction costs at small size
questions.explain: Market impact grows with order size relative to available liquidity. At a small enough size, the order barely moves the market, so a backtest never sees the cost that would emerge if the same strategy traded at real institutional scale.

questions.q: What does a strategy's 'capacity' refer to?
options: The number of different instruments a strategy trades
The maximum amount of capital a strategy can deploy before net-of-cost performance degrades below being worth trading
The number of lines of code required to implement the strategy
The amount of historical data available for backtesting
questions.explain: Capacity is the capital ceiling at which modeled transaction costs and market impact erode the strategy's gross edge to roughly zero (or below an acceptable hurdle), beyond which deploying more capital isn't worthwhile.

questions.q: Why might a strategy trading illiquid small-cap stocks have a much lower capacity than one trading large-cap equities or major FX pairs, even with an identical underlying signal?
options: Illiquid instruments have no transaction costs
Illiquid instruments have lower average daily volume, so the same order size represents a much larger fraction of ADV, driving up market impact cost at a much smaller capital level
Large-cap equities cannot be traded by small funds
Capacity has nothing to do with liquidity
questions.explain: Because impact scales with the fraction of ADV traded, a fixed dollar order represents a much bigger participation rate in a thinly traded instrument, pushing impact costs up — and the capacity ceiling down — much sooner than in a highly liquid instrument.
